body:
How merchants contributed to Jain heritage

Jain temples and religious institutions in Gujarat received support from a variety of donors. Merchants and wealthy householders were particularly important because commercial prosperity provided resources that could be devoted to religious and charitable purposes.

Donors might finance the construction or repair of temples, commission sacred images, maintain facilities for pilgrims or support religious teachers. Such donations brought together several groups: patrons provided resources, artisans carried out construction and decoration, and religious communities used and maintained the institutions.

Trade centres and pilgrimage centres could reinforce one another. A prosperous commercial community might support a temple, while an established pilgrimage centre attracted visitors and generated demand for local services. This connection helps explain why the history of Jainism in Gujarat is closely associated with both towns and sacred sites.

Vimal Shah and the Vimala Vasahi temple

Vimal Shah was a minister associated with the Chaulukya ruler Bhima I of Gujarat. He is remembered as the patron of the Vimala Vasahi Jain temple at Dilwara, Mount Abu, constructed around 1031–1032 CE.

Vimala Vasahi is dedicated to Adinatha, the 1st Tirthankara. It is celebrated for its finely carved marble architecture. Its comparatively restrained exterior contrasts with richly decorated interior spaces, including elaborately carved ceilings and pillars.

Vastupala, Tejapala and Luna Vasahi

Vastupala and Tejapala were influential ministerial patrons associated with the later political history of Gujarat. They are remembered for supporting Jain architecture and religious institutions.

The Luna Vasahi temple at Dilwara, built around 1230 CE, is associated especially with Tejapala and the brothers' patronage. It is dedicated to Neminatha, the 22nd Tirthankara. Like Vimala Vasahi, it is known for exceptionally detailed marble carving.

Remember the present-day location

Dilwara is at Mount Abu in Rajasthan, not Gujarat. It is relevant to Gujarat's Jain heritage because its major patrons were historically connected with the ruling and ministerial circles of Gujarat.

A comparison of major patrons and temples

Continued merchant patronage in Ahmedabad

Jain temple patronage continued after the medieval period. An important later example is the Hutheesing Jain Temple in Ahmedabad, built in 1848 CE through the patronage of the wealthy merchant Sheth Hutheesing.

The temple is dedicated to Dharmanatha, the 15th Tirthankara. Its finely worked stone architecture also demonstrates the continuing contribution of skilled building and carving communities, including the Salat artisans.

Hutheesing Temple belongs to the 19th century, so it should not be confused chronologically with the Chaulukya-period temples. Its relevance is that it demonstrates the continued tradition of Jain merchant patronage in Gujarat.

Architectural and economic impact

Jain donations contributed to the construction of durable religious monuments and to the development of specialised craftsmanship. Temple complexes required the work of stone carvers, builders, sculptors and other artisans. Religious endowments also helped sustain institutions over time.

Temple patronage was not exclusively a royal activity. Some of the best-known Jain monuments were financed by ministers and wealthy merchants. This is an important distinction when identifying the patrons of individual buildings.

Prelims focus

  • Vimal Shah patronised Vimala Vasahi at Dilwara around 1031–1032 CE.
  • Vimala Vasahi is dedicated to Adinatha, the 1st Tirthankara.
  • Vastupala and Tejapala are associated with Luna Vasahi, built around 1230 CE.
  • Luna Vasahi is dedicated to Neminatha, the 22nd Tirthankara.
  • Hutheesing Temple in Ahmedabad was built in 1848 CE and is dedicated to Dharmanatha, the 15th Tirthankara.
  • Trap: Dilwara is in present-day Rajasthan, although its principal medieval patrons had strong connections with Gujarat.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class 7, Chapter 6, 'Towns, Traders and Craftspersons,' printed pp. 76–81; NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 6, 'Temple Architecture and Sculpture,' printed p. 95; University of Notre Dame, Hesburgh Libraries, 'Dilwara Temple Complex: Luna Vasahi Temple,' architectural collection description, consulted 18 November 2026; District Administration, Ahmedabad, 'Hathee Singh Temple,' consulted 18 November 2026.]

body:
Why Valabhi is important

Valabhi, also written Vallabhi, was an important centre of learning in early medieval Gujarat. In Jain history, it is especially associated with the compilation and written preservation of the Shvetambara Jain canonical texts.

The historical importance of Valabhi should be understood through the distinction between the original teachings of Mahavira and the later preservation of those teachings in written form. Mahavira lived many centuries before the major textual compilation associated with Valabhi.

From oral teaching to written manuscripts

Mahavira's teachings were initially transmitted by his disciples and their successors through oral instruction. Oral transmission depended on teachers and communities preserving and repeating what they had learned.

Over time, Jain communities developed collections of religious texts dealing with conduct, doctrine, discipline and other aspects of religious life. These collections are commonly referred to as Agamas.

As teachings passed through generations, preserving them in written form became increasingly important. Written manuscripts could be copied and maintained by religious communities, helping later generations study and transmit the texts.

The council associated with Valabhi

According to Shvetambara Jain tradition, an important council was held at Valabhi in approximately the 5th–6th century CE. It is associated with the Jain teacher Devardhigani Kshamashramana.

The council is remembered for collecting, arranging and committing important Shvetambara canonical teachings to writing. It was therefore a major event in the preservation of Jain religious literature.

Which Jain canon was involved?

The Valabhi compilation is associated particularly with the Shvetambara tradition. It should not be described as the single universally accepted scriptural canon of all Jain sects. Digambara Jain traditions have a different understanding of the survival of the earliest scriptures and developed their own authoritative literature.

Important chronological distinction

The approximate sequence is straightforward:

  1. 6th century BCE: the period in which Mahavira taught, according to the broad historical chronology used in school textbooks.
  2. Following centuries: Jain teachings continued to be transmitted orally and developed into organised textual traditions.
  3. Approximately 5th–6th century CE: the important Shvetambara canonical compilation associated with Valabhi took place.
  4. Later centuries: religious manuscripts continued to be copied, studied and preserved in Jain libraries and other repositories.

This sequence explains why the date of a surviving manuscript need not be the date when its religious teaching first originated. A text written on paper centuries later may preserve material from a much older tradition.

Valabhi's cultural significance

The Valabhi tradition places Gujarat within the history of Indian religious literature. It shows that Gujarat was not only a region of Jain temples and pilgrimage sites; it was also connected with the organisation and preservation of important religious texts.

The work associated with Valabhi also helps explain the importance of later Jain manuscript libraries. A written religious tradition requires continued copying, preservation and study. These activities became an important part of Gujarat's cultural heritage.

Prelims focus

  • Valabhi or Vallabhi was an important centre of learning in Gujarat.
  • It is associated with the compilation of Shvetambara Jain canonical literature.
  • The major council is generally placed in approximately the 5th–6th century CE.
  • Devardhigani Kshamashramana is associated with the Valabhi compilation.
  • Mahavira's teachings were transmitted orally before their later written compilation.
  • Trap: Valabhi was not the birthplace of Jainism, and its compilation should not be treated as the universally accepted canon of every Jain sect.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 7, 'New Questions and Ideas,' printed p. 70; Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, discussion of Jain religious literature and the Valabhi council; Satyaranjan Banerjee, Introducing Jainism, discussion of the Shvetambara council at Valabhi, printed p. 22; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Chapter 4, 'Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings,' printed p. 89.]

title: Valabhi and the Preservation of the Jain Canon

body:
What is a Jain bhandara?

A Jain bhandara is a repository or library where manuscripts and other written works are kept. Such collections often developed in association with Jain religious institutions, temples and centres of learning.

Their purpose was to preserve material that could be read, copied, studied and transmitted. The collections included religious literature, commentaries and works connected with wider fields of learning.

The survival of Jain manuscripts depended on the work of several groups: scholars who produced or explained texts, scribes who copied them, donors who financed their preparation, and institutions that preserved the written material.

Important manuscript centres in Gujarat

Gujarat became an important region for Jain manuscript preservation. Collections and institutions associated with this history include:

  • Patan: an important historical centre of Jain learning and manuscript preservation, including the Shri Hemchandracharya Jain Gyan Mandir.
  • Khambhat or Cambay: a historic trading town associated with Jain manuscript repositories and religious institutions.
  • Ahmedabad: an important centre for the study and preservation of Jain and other Indian manuscripts, including the L. D. Institute of Indology.

These places should not be confused with Valabhi. Valabhi is especially associated with a major early medieval canonical compilation, whereas Patan, Khambhat and Ahmedabad are important for manuscript collections and the continued study or preservation of texts.

Materials used for manuscripts

Earlier Indian manuscripts were often written on palm leaves. Paper became an important writing material in later manuscript traditions. The physical form of a manuscript therefore provides useful context for recognising different examples of Jain literary heritage.

A manuscript could contain only text or could combine writing with painted illustrations. Illustrations were particularly important in some Jain manuscripts produced in western India.

The Western Indian school of miniature painting

Miniature paintings are small-scale paintings made with fine detail. In western India, illustrated Jain manuscripts became an important part of this artistic tradition.

Illustrated manuscripts were produced on materials such as palm leaves and paper. Their painted scenes helped communicate religious narratives and made the manuscripts objects of artistic as well as literary importance.

Western Indian Jain manuscript paintings are often recognised by strong colours, stylised human figures, angular forms and prominent eyes. Individual works vary, so these features describe a broad artistic tradition rather than an unchanging rule followed by every painter.

The Kalpa Sutra tradition

The Kalpa Sutra is an important text in the Shvetambara Jain tradition and includes material concerning the lives of Tirthankaras and religious teachers. It became a major subject of Jain manuscript illustration.

An especially clear historical example is a Kalpa Sutra and Kalakacharyakatha manuscript dated 1411, identified as originating in Gujarat and preserved in the Smithsonian's National Museum of Asian Art collection. It is made on paper and uses opaque watercolour, ink and gold.

This example demonstrates that by the early 15th century Gujarat had an established tradition of producing richly illustrated Jain manuscripts. Its date is the date of that manuscript, not the date when the religious narratives themselves first originated.

Why copying and patronage mattered

Preparing manuscripts required writing materials, skilled scribes and, where illustrations were included, painters. Patrons could support the production of new copies, while religious institutions could preserve completed works.

Through this activity, Jain communities contributed to the development of literary culture and painting in Gujarat. The manuscript tradition also helped preserve religious teachings across generations.

Prelims focus

  • A Jain bhandara is a manuscript repository or library.
  • Patan is associated with the Shri Hemchandracharya Jain Gyan Mandir.
  • Khambhat or Cambay is another historical centre associated with Jain manuscript collections.
  • Western Indian miniature painting includes illustrated Jain manuscripts.
  • A Gujarat manuscript of the Kalpa Sutra and Kalakacharyakatha dated 1411 is preserved in the National Museum of Asian Art collection.
  • Trap: The date of a manuscript copy is not necessarily the date of the original teaching or text.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class 7, Chapter 9, 'The Making of Regional Cultures,' section 'Painting for Patrons: The Tradition of Miniatures,' printed p. 128; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Chapter 4, 'Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings,' printed p. 89; Indira Gandhi National Centre for the Arts, Survey of Manuscripts in India, Gujarat institutions table; Smithsonian National Museum of Asian Art, collection record 'Kalpa Sutra and Kalakacharyakatha,' dated 1411, consulted 18 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Manuscript production connected scholars, scribes, painters, donors and libraries.

title: Jain Manuscript Libraries and the Western Indian Painting Tradition
